# Benchmark: Rampa and other accessibility checkers

How does Rampa compare with the checkers people already use? This page answers with measurements, not with what each tool's documentation says: the same pages, the same browser, the same scoring, for every tool. Everything is in [bench/](../bench): one command runs it again (`cd bench && node run.mjs --docs`), and the raw results of each run are kept in `bench/results/<date>/`.

## Reading the results

Written from the run of 2026-10-11; the tables above and below are regenerated by each run, this section is not.


**The final run.** Rampa's three rows were run again on 2026-10-11 at `ebd4d07`, after the last coverage waves were merged; the other tools' rows are the first run's (their versions did not change), on the same pages and pairs. The rerun reused the first run's judgment cache: 2,662 of 2,669 model answers came from it, since no judged criterion's prompt changed, so the rerun's time per page for the Gemma rows (0.86 s) is not the cost of a cold run; the first run, with an empty cache, measured about 4 seconds a page. Two pages of the probes row did not load within 30 s and stay unchecked.
- **The rule engines are close to each other.** On the failed examples, axe-core, Alfa, QualWeb and Rampa without a model caught between 63% and 67%, with overlapping intervals; IBM and Pa11y's axe runner a little less, and Pa11y with its default runner, HTML_CodeSniffer, 19%. Precision separates them more: axe-core, Rampa and Alfa stayed between 0.87 and 0.93, while IBM and QualWeb failed many passed and inapplicable examples under 1.3.1 (IBM's content-outside-landmarks rule, QualWeb's data-table techniques H39, H51 and H63) and landed near 0.7.
- **Rampa without a model is axe-core.** Same engine, same version. Its own rules are experimental and report below the default threshold, so it caught exactly what axe-core caught (178 of 284). It has two false positives fewer: axe-core's 2.5.3 label mismatches on two inapplicable examples, which differ only by a hyphen or a shortened word and which Rampa sends to review instead.
- **What the model adds at the default threshold is modest.** Gemma caught 15 more failed examples (193 of 284): alternatives that do not describe their image (1.1.1), page and part languages that do not match the text (3.1.1, 3.1.2), and links whose text says nothing in its context (2.4.4, three failed examples of 5effbb). It added two false positives, both an empty `autocomplete` on a username field that 73f2c2 leaves out of scope and that [criteria.md](criteria.md) argues is a real 1.3.5 failure. All of the gain is on rules Rampa was tuned on; on the other rules, Rampa + Gemma and axe-core scored the same.
- **Counted the way `rampa eval` counts**, with findings below the threshold, Rampa + Gemma caught 227 of 284 (0.80) at precision 0.88: almost every failed example of 1.1.1, 2.4.4 and 2.4.6, with 16 more false positives, six of them ACT page titles such as "Passed Example 3". Judgments of ordinary titles, link texts and headings sit below the threshold because, on real pages, they were mostly wrong ([the re-measurement](studies/real-pages-2026-10-remeasure.md)); the ACT pages reward them.
- **Probes add nothing at the default threshold**: every probe is experimental. Counted with low confidence, they caught failed examples under five more criteria (1.3.4 orientation, 1.4.2 audio control, 2.1.2 keyboard trap, 2.1.4 character key shortcuts, 2.4.7 focus visible) and all 12 of 1.4.4 (resize text), for 21 criteria with a true failure, the most of any row, at about 20 seconds a page.
- **Pairs.** No rule engine told more than 4 of the 96 pairs apart; QualWeb's 4 are labels moved into `aria-label` and off the screen (3.3.2), which its check for `label` elements (QW-WCAG-T17) catches. Rampa + Gemma told 47 apart at the default threshold and 73 with low confidence counted: the 21 link pairs (link text made generic, or pointed elsewhere) show only below the threshold, by design since the real-page study. Nobody told apart the 17 pairs of criteria Rampa judges only on request (1.3.1, 1.3.3, 1.4.5, 2.5.3), which its default run does not judge.
- **What no tool caught.** No row caught a failed example of 1.2.1, 1.2.3 or 1.2.5 (alternatives for media), 1.3.3 (sensory characteristics), 1.4.5 (images of text), 2.2.2 (pause, stop, hide) or 3.3.1 (error identification). Rampa has judgment modules for 1.3.3, 1.4.5 and 3.3.1, but they run only on request and were not run here.
- **Time.** On these tiny pages, the rule engines took 0.5 to 1.2 seconds a page, Rampa without a model 0.7, with Gemma about 4, with probes about 20, and Lighthouse about 6.
- **Lighthouse and Pa11y's axe runner are not axe-core plus something.** On the sample, every Lighthouse failure was an axe-core violation of the same rule on the same page except `target-size`, which Lighthouse turns on and axe-core 4.14 leaves off by default; Lighthouse ran fewer rules and returned nothing on pages that paint nothing. Pa11y's axe runner levels results by impact, so axe-core's "needs review" results for skip links, captions and contrast became Pa11y errors, and it never reported `label-content-name-mismatch` (2.5.3: 0 of 16, where axe-core caught 16).

## What is measured

1. **The W3C ACT test cases.** Every [ACT rule](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/act/rules/) that maps to a WCAG 2.2 A or AA success criterion for conformance, and every one of its HTML test cases: passed, failed and inapplicable examples, with the outcome the ACT Task Force published. For each tool and each test case: did the tool report a failure under the criterion the rule maps to? From that: failed examples caught (recall), passed and inapplicable examples flagged (false positives), precision and F1, overall and per criterion.
2. **Rampa's corrupted pairs.** A passed test page next to a copy broken on purpose: an `alt` turned into `img-1`, a title into "Welcome", a `lang` into another valid language, a label moved off the screen. Which tools fail the copy and not the original?
3. **Coverage.** How many WCAG 2.2 A/AA criteria each tool reported at least one true failure for, next to how many it claims and how many it failed anything under.
4. **Time per page**, on one machine.

## The tools

| Row | What runs | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| axe-core | [axe-core](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core) 4.14.0 (Deque, MPL-2.0), the version Rampa ships, with every rule it enables by default | through Deque's [@axe-core/playwright](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@axe-core/playwright), which runs it in every frame |
| Lighthouse | [Lighthouse](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/lighthouse) 13.5.0 (Google, Apache-2.0), accessibility category, desktop preset | on a sample only; see below |
| Pa11y | [Pa11y](https://github.com/pa11y/pa11y) 10.0.0 (LGPL-3.0) with its default runner, HTML_CodeSniffer (Pa11y's fork, 2.6.0), standard WCAG2AA | Pa11y's own Puppeteer, pointed at the same Edge |
| Pa11y (axe) | the same Pa11y with its axe runner | its own axe-core, 4.13.0 |
| IBM | [IBM Equal Access](https://github.com/IBMa/equal-access) rule engine (accessibility-checker-engine 4.0.34, Apache-2.0), policy IBM_Accessibility, the default of the `accessibility-checker` package | injected in the page, as `accessibility-checker` does |
| Alfa | [Siteimprove Alfa](https://github.com/Siteimprove/alfa) open-source rules (@siteimprove/alfa-rules 0.119.0, MIT), the default set | through @siteimprove/alfa-playwright, audited with no one to answer its questions |
| QualWeb | [QualWeb](https://github.com/qualweb/qualweb) core 0.9.5 (ISC) with the modules its command line runs by default: ACT rules, WCAG techniques, best practices | QualWeb's own Puppeteer, pointed at the same Edge |
| Rampa | this repository's `dist/cli.mjs`, `rampa check --no-llm`: axe-core, Rampa's own rules | one `rampa check` per 20 pages |
| Rampa + Gemma | `rampa check --model ollama:gemma4:12b`: the eight criteria Rampa judges by default, on Gemma 4 12B through a local Ollama | the same |
| Rampa + Gemma + probes | the same with `--probe all`: probes that drive the page (zoom, reflow, text spacing, keyboard, focus, media, hover, orientation, shortcuts, color, states) | rerun only on the test cases of criteria a probe checks; the other pages keep the row above |

**Not run.**

- **WAVE** (WebAIM). From a script, its engine runs through WebAIM's paid API (per credit, with 100 free credits for a new account) or a stand-alone engine WebAIM provides separately; the free WAVE is a website and browser extensions that show their results to a person, in the page. The benchmark runs only what is free and local.
- **ARC Toolkit** (TPGi). A browser extension with no command line or API.
- **Lighthouse on every page.** Lighthouse's accessibility audits are axe-core rules, run by the axe-core Lighthouse depends on (the same 4.14.0 here) with a list of rules of its own. It took several times as long per page as axe-core (the time table below), and it ends its run with no audits at all (`NO_FCP`) on a page that paints nothing, which some ACT pages are. So it ran on the first three test cases of each rule, to show what it adds to axe-core: the results are in "Lighthouse against axe-core" below. axe-core stands for it in the tables.
- **The `accessibility-checker` npm package itself.** It runs the IBM engine above through its own Puppeteer, and by default downloads the engine from the jsDelivr CDN at run time (rule archive "latest"). The benchmark injects the pinned engine package instead, with the same default policy, so the version is fixed and the browser is the shared one.

QualWeb installed and ran; its core still depends on Puppeteer 22, which npm marks as deprecated.

Versions were the latest published releases when the benchmark was set up (October 2026) that were old enough for pnpm's minimum release age policy, pinned exactly in [bench/package.json](../bench/package.json) with their own lockfile.

## Method

**Test cases.** The ACT test case file (`testcases.json`) is the one `rampa eval` uses, read through Rampa's own build (`dist/eval/index.mjs`) and identified by its SHA-256 in each run. A rule is kept when one of its accessibility requirements is a WCAG 2.x success criterion of level A or AA in WCAG 2.2, marked `forConformance` (a criterion listed only as secondary, such as the 1.3.1 of the ARIA rules, does not count). Left out, for every tool alike:

- the two device-motion rules of 2.5.4 (c249d5, 7677a9): their outcome depends on moving the device, and no tool here can;
- the SVG and XML test cases of the rules kept: `rampa eval` loads only HTML documents;
- rules that map to no A/AA criterion for conformance (AAA only, or WAI-ARIA and technique requirements only).

The full list is under "ACT rules left out" in the results.

**Units.** A test case of a rule that maps to two criteria (link name, c487ae: 2.4.4 and 4.1.2; image button name, 59796f: 1.1.1 and 4.1.2) is scored once under each, and a failed example fails both. Each (test case, criterion) is a unit.

**What counts as a failure.** Only what the tool itself calls a failure, in its own terms: axe-core's violations, Pa11y's errors, IBM's violations, Alfa's failed outcomes, QualWeb's failed assertions, Rampa's findings at or above its default confidence threshold. What a tool leaves to a person (axe-core's incomplete results, Pa11y's warnings, IBM's potential violations and manual checks, Alfa's "can't tell", QualWeb's warnings, Rampa's findings below the threshold and items to review) is counted apart, as review, and a second table shows the scores if review counted as failure. Advice is counted neither way: HTML_CodeSniffer's notices (it raises a "Check that…" notice for most criteria on every page), IBM's recommendations and QualWeb's best practices. Each tool's failures are mapped to WCAG criteria by its own metadata: axe-core's `wcag###` tags, the criterion in each HTML_CodeSniffer code, the IBM rule set's checkpoints, Alfa's rule requirements, QualWeb's success-criteria metadata, and for Rampa the criterion of each finding plus each criterion's status in its report (a finding names one criterion, but an axe-core rule mapped to two, such as `link-name` for 2.4.4 and 4.1.2, makes both "failures" there, as axe-core's tags do). No mapping was written by hand.

**Rampa's confidence threshold.** `rampa check` fails a run only on findings at or above its default confidence threshold (medium). Experimental checks, every probe among them, and judgments of titles, link texts and headings that are not on Rampa's lists of generic text are reported below it: listed with `--verbose`, never failing a build. The tables count them as review, and add a reading of the same runs with them counted as failures, which is how `rampa eval` scores and how the README's evaluation numbers were made.

**Scoring.** A unit is caught when its case is a failed example and the tool failed its criterion on that page; a false positive when its case is a passed or inapplicable example and the tool failed its criterion. Every tool is scored on every criterion, including those it does not check; the coverage table then scores each tool on the criteria it failed anything under. A page a tool could not check counts as nothing reported, and those pages are counted.

**Pairs.** The pairs are exactly those `rampa eval` builds, for every criterion that has a corruptor (also the criteria Rampa judges only on request). `rampa eval` breaks the page inside its own browser; the other tools only take a URL. So each half is built once in Edge (the intact page as loaded, and the page after Rampa's corruptor ran on it), saved as HTML, and served by a local server at the test page's own path, with every other request passed to www.w3.org. Every tool, Rampa included, checks the same two saved pages. Scripts already ran when a half was saved, so they are kept inert in both halves. A pair counts as told apart when the tool fails the corrupted half under the pair's criterion and not the intact one.

**Same browser.** Microsoft Edge, headless, the same executable for every tool: Playwright drives it for axe-core, IBM, Alfa and Rampa; Puppeteer for Pa11y, QualWeb and Lighthouse. Each tool keeps its own defaults for everything else: viewport, and what it waits for before testing (`load` for the tools the harness drives, the network going idle for Pa11y, Rampa's own settle).

**Time.** Measured on the same machine, one tool at a time, two pages at a time. The machine was also running other work, including other jobs on the same GPU, so read the times as orders of magnitude. The probes row reads its judgments from the cache the Gemma row filled, so its time is collection and probes, not the model.

**Network.** The ACT pages load from www.w3.org. When the connection dropped during a run, the pages that failed to load for that reason were checked again afterwards (`node run.mjs --retry-errors`); the pages a tool still could not check are listed under the results.

### Time per page

Wall time from opening the page to the tool's results, on this machine, with the pages of one tool at a time. For the in-process tools that is a new browser context, navigation and the analysis; for Rampa, one `rampa check` process per 20 pages, timed between consecutive reports (collection, axe-core, its rules, judgments, probes). The first page of each Rampa process also starts Node and the browser: it is left out of the median and shown apart. ACT pages are tiny, so these are lower bounds for real pages.

### False positives the engines share

### Lighthouse against axe-core, page by page

On 150 pages both checked (the first 3 test cases of each rule): 1 page had a Lighthouse failure axe-core did not report (act:9bd38c:5c97d7f0e034132669260719d7ea5ae899990ad4: target-size). axe-core WCAG failures Lighthouse did not report: `frame-focusable-content` (1), `scrollable-region-focusable` (1), `document-title` (1). Lighthouse returned no audits on 18 pages (Lighthouse CHROME_INTERSTITIAL_ERROR, The "start lh:storage:clearBrowserCaches" performance mark has not been set, Lighthouse NO_FCP).

### Pa11y's axe runner against axe-core, page by page

On 1009 pages both checked. Pa11y errors that axe-core itself left incomplete: `bypass` (137), `video-caption` (32), `color-contrast` (26), `frame-title-unique` (8), `th-has-data-cells` (5), `aria-valid-attr-value` (4), `aria-hidden-focus` (2), `aria-required-children` (1). axe-core WCAG violations Pa11y reported as a warning or notice: `meta-viewport` (5); and not at all: `label-content-name-mismatch` (18), `frame-focusable-content` (3), `link-in-text-block` (1).

## Caveats

- **Rampa plays at home.** Rampa's judgment prompts were tuned while reading the errors of these same ACT test cases, and several of its rules and probes were built against them. The "home advantage" table splits the scores: a rule counts as home when Rampa's source or tests mention its id, a deliberately wide reading (37 of the 56 rules) that also takes in rules Rampa leaves to axe-core, such as the syntax sets of `rampa eval`. The rule engines have their own home advantage: axe-core, Alfa, QualWeb and IBM implement ACT rules and test against these test cases, and their ACT implementation reports are published by W3C. Neither kind of tuning says how a tool does on pages it was not tuned on.
- **The corrupted pairs are Rampa's design.** They break exactly what Rampa judges (meaning, not syntax): no rule engine is expected to tell them apart, and that is what they show. The words the corruptions use are not in Rampa's prompts.
- **ACT pages are tiny.** A test case is a few elements built to show one rule. On real pages, Rampa's judgment has been measured to be much noisier: in the [held-out real-page re-measurement](studies/real-pages-2026-10-remeasure.md), precision of its judged findings was 0.38 at the default threshold and 0.19 with low-confidence findings, labelled by two LLM judges, not by people. Treat the precision here as an upper bound for every tool.
- **A false positive is under a criterion, not a rule.** A passed example of one rule can still fail the same criterion for another reason the rule does not test (a page with no skip link under 2.4.1, an image without `alt` on a page about link names). A tool that checks more under a criterion can be "wrong" here and right about the page. The table "False positives the engines share" counts, for each tool, the false positives that at least three other independent engines also report.
- **Failure and warning mean different things in each tool.** The review table shows how much the picture moves when review items count. IBM's checker fails a scan on potential violations by default, and Pa11y's axe runner calls an axe-core result an error by its impact, so some of its errors are results axe-core itself left for review.
- **Published outcomes.** Every tool is scored against the outcomes in the published ACT file. Rampa's own `rampa eval` scores one 0va7u6 case (an image of the word "Welcome" next to the text "Welcome to our website") as passed, following the rule's proposed version; here it is a failed example, as published.
- **What Rampa ran.** The Gemma rows judge the eight default criteria; 1.3.1, 1.3.3, 1.4.5, 2.5.3 and 3.3.1 are judged only on request, so their cases and pairs count against Rampa's default configuration. A single run of a local model at temperature 0 on a shared GPU: another run can differ by a few cases.
- **Saved pair pages.** A saved page loses what only a live page has: event handlers, script timers, and what a script or a corruptor changed inside a frame (a frame loads its own page again). Both halves lose it alike, so a pair still differs only by the corruption, except where the 1.3.3 corruption reaches into a frame (it can, on the one 9bd38c page that has a frame); and a tool may treat a saved page slightly differently from the original test page. `pairs.json` lists the pages that had scripts or frames.
